propositions.text: The principal claimant, his wife (the claimant), and their child claim Ethiopian citizenship and refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, (the "principal claimant" ), his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the "co-claimant" hereinafter called the claimant) and their child XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the minor claimant) claim to be citizens of Ethiopia and seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant, his wife, and child claim Ethiopian citizenship and refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1) (applicant).

propositions.text: The minor claimant's designated representative was appointed on September 18, 2009; the principal claimant agreed to act as representative at the hearing.
propositions.quote: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX was appointed the Designated Representative of the minor claimant on September 18, 2009. At the hearing, the principal claimant confirmed his agreement to act as his daughter's designated representative.

paragraphs.summary: The minor claimant's designated representative was appointed September 18, 2009; principal claimant agreed to act as representative (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The principal claimant was born in Ethiopia in 1974; the claimant in 1977; the minor claimant was born in Paris in 2008.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant was born in XXXXX XXXXX, Ethiopia on XXXXXX, 1974. The claimant was born in XXXXX XXXXX on XXXXXX, 1977. The minor claimant was born in Paris, France on XXXXXX, 2008.

paragraphs.summary: The principal claimant was born in Ethiopia in 1974; claimant in 1977; minor claimant born in Paris in 2008 (applicant).

propositions.text: The principal claimant and minor claimant depend on the claimant's claim; all are Ethiopian citizens.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant and the minor claimant depend upon the claim of the claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX. The claimant alleges the following. The principal claimant, the claimant and the minor claimant are citizens of Ethiopia.

propositions.text: The claimant's father lived in France 30 years and was a leader of an Ethiopian political group.
propositions.quote: The claimant's father, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, who resided in France for the past thirty years, was a XXXXX XXXX of an XXXXX XXXXX XXXX, the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.

propositions.text: The principal claimant and claimant married in 2005; claimant moved to France in 2005 for a position at an Ethiopian headquarters in Paris.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant and the claimant were married XXXXX 2005. In XXXX 2005 the claimant moved to France to take up the position of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (XXXXX) headquarters in Paris, France.

propositions.text: Claimant lived with her father in Paris; principal claimant joined her the next year.
propositions.quote: The claimant lived with her father in Paris. The principal claimant joined the claimant in Paris the following year.

propositions.text: After claimant arrived in Paris, changes occurred in Ethiopian staff; senior staff learned claimant was her father's daughter; Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs questioned her recruitment.
propositions.quote: Soon after the claimant arrived in Paris in 2005, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX which caused many changes in the Ethiopian staff in Paris at that time. Shortly after, senior staff came to know that the claimant was the daughter of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The matter was reported to the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and questions were asked regarding the recruitment of the claimant to a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant and family are Ethiopian citizens; claimant's father was a political leader in France; claimant moved to Paris in 2005; her relationship to her father became known and questioned (applicant).

propositions.text: Claimant worked at Ethiopian embassy in Paris when short staffed; was asked to promote political ideology but refused.
propositions.quote: At times, the claimant was required to work at the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris when they were short staffed. The claimant was requested to work to gain support for the XXXXX XXXXX among the Ethiopians working at the XXXXX Headquarters. She was unwilling to promote the political ideology of the XXXXX XXXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant was accused of assisting her father politically; her husband traveled to Ethiopia with political writings in 2009.
propositions.quote: The claimant was accused of assisting her father in his political writing. It was discovered that her husband had travelled to Ethiopia in 2009 with XXXXX XXXX XXXXX political writings.

propositions.text: In 2009, claimant learned her and her family's names were on a list compiled by Ethiopian embassy in Paris.
propositions.quote: In 2009, the claimant learned that her name, her husband's name and her father's name were on a list compiled by the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris. The list named XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant worked at Ethiopian embassy, refused to promote ideology, was accused of assisting father; family names were listed by embassy in 2009 (applicant).

propositions.text: Claimant was accused of not convincing embassy to release funds; she faced verbal abuse, warnings, and intimidation.
propositions.quote: The claimant was accused of not convincing XXXXX to release funds for Ethiopian projects. Her inaction was blamed on her political beliefs. She received verbal abuse, warnings and intimidation in regard to this matter each time she XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant was accused of failing to secure funds and faced verbal abuse and intimidation (applicant).

propositions.text: Claimant received letter in 2009 from Ethiopian embassy terminating employment and instructing her to report to Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: The claimant received a letter dated XXXX, 2009 from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris informing her that her employment was terminated and she was instructed to travel to Ethiopia and report to the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX by XXXXX, 2009.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant received letter in 2009 terminating employment and instructing return to Ethiopia (applicant).

propositions.text: Claimant and family traveled to Canada on holiday in 2009; claimant learned she would be interrogated and tortured if returned to Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: The claimant, principal claimant and minor claimant travelled to Canada on a holiday. They arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2009. While on holiday, the claimant learned, through a friend of a friend who works at the XXXXX XXXXX office in XXXXX XXXXX, that, upon her return to Ethiopia, the claimant would be interrogated about her father's political activities. She understood that the interrogation would include torture and imprisonment.

propositions.text: Claimant's family in Ethiopia received calls from unknown individuals asking about her return.
propositions.quote: She heard from her family in Ethiopia that they had received telephone calls from unknown individuals requesting information on the claimant's return to Ethiopia.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant and family traveled to Canada on holiday; claimant learned she would face interrogation and torture if returned; family received inquiries about her return (applicant).

propositions.text: Claimant and family made refugee protection claims on September 1, 2009.
propositions.quote: The claimant, principal claimant and minor claimant made claims for refugee protection on September 1, 2009.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant and family made refugee protection claims on September 1, 2009 (applicant).

propositions.text: After arrival in Canada, claimant's son was born in 2010; claimant's father died in early 2010.
propositions.quote: Subsequent to their arrival in Canada, the principal claimant's and claimant's son, XXXXX XXXXX, was born on XXXXX, 2010. The claimant's father, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, died in early XXXXX, 2010.

paragraphs.summary: After arrival in Canada, claimant's son was born and claimant's father died in early 2010 (applicant).

propositions.text: The panel finds the principal claimant, claimant, and minor claimant are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, (the "principal claimant" ), his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the claimant) and their child, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the minor claimant), are not Convention refugees pursuant to s. 96 of the IRPA, nor are they persons in need of protection, pursuant to s. 97(1) of IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The hearing issues were credibility, failure to claim in France, and identity.
propositions.quote: The issues in this hearing were: * Credibility * Failure to claim in France Identity

paragraphs.summary: The hearing issues were credibility, failure to claim in France, and identity (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The panel finds on balance of probabilities that the principal claimant and claimant are who they say and are Ethiopian citizens, supported by passports and birth certificates.
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant is who he says he is and that he is a citizen of Ethiopia. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is who she says she is and that she is a citizen of Ethiopia. In support of their identities, each provided a copy of their Ethiopian passport2 and birth certificate.3

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds principal claimant and claimant are who they say and Ethiopian citizens, supported by passports and birth certificates (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The minor claimant was born in France to foreign parents, left before age two, and French nationality applies only at majority or with application.
propositions.quote: The minor claimant was born in Paris, France. A copy of her birth certificate was provided to the panel.4 She was born to foreign parents and left France before the age of two years. The claimant provided a copy of a document, 'Council of Europe, France, Legislative provisions Concerning Nationality',5 which states: "Since 1 September 1998 children born in France to foreign parents born abroad acquire French nationality ipso jure when they reach the age of majority or may themselves apply for French nationality as of 16 years of age; alternately, their legal representative may lodge an application with their consent once they have reached the age of 13."

paragraphs.summary: The minor claimant was born in France to foreign parents, left before age two, and French nationality applies only at majority or with application (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: The panel finds the minor claimant is Ethiopian citizen, supported by passport and birth certificate.
propositions.quote: The panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the minor claimant is a citizen of Ethiopia. In support of her identity, a copy of her passport6 was provided as well as her birth certificate previously mentioned.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the minor claimant is Ethiopian citizen, supported by passport and birth certificate (earlier decision-maker).

propositions.text: Claimant's sworn testimony is presumed truthful unless valid reason to doubt exists.
propositions.quote: The sworn testimony of the claimant is presumed to be truthful unless there is valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.7

propositions.text: Claimant failed to provide consistent or credible evidence; cumulative effect negates claim.
propositions.quote: Nonetheless, the panel finds that the claimant has failed to advance her claim with evidence that is consistent or credible. The panel is aware that none of the credibility concerns raised here may be sufficient, each on its own, to negate this claim. However, the cumulative effect of all of them is that the panel does not have sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that the claimant is a Convention refugee.

propositions.text: A general finding of lack of credibility may extend to all relevant testimony, per Court of Appeal in Sheikh.
propositions.quote: As the Court of Appeal in Sheikh,8 MacGuigan, J.A. held: even without disbelieving every word [a claimant] has uttered, a ... panel may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes that there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim ... In other words, a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may concurrently extend to all relevant information emanating from his testimony.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's testimony presumed truthful but found cumulatively not credible; Court of Appeal in Sheikh supports general credibility findings (earlier decision-maker and prior court).

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant's relationship to father caused embassy to require her return to Ethiopia in 2009.
propositions.quote: The panel is not persuaded that the relationship between the claimant and her father, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, was a reason for XXXXX XXXXX to require her to return to Ethiopia from Paris in 2009.

propositions.text: Credibility requires evidence to be probably so, not just possibly so, per Justice Mahoney in Orelien.
propositions.quote: The panel is guided by the words of Mr. Justice Mahoney in Orelien9 wherein he stated: It seems to me one cannot be satisfied the evidence is credible or trustworthy unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so.

paragraphs.summary: Panel not persuaded claimant's relationship to father caused return order; credibility requires probable truth, per Orelien (earlier decision-maker and prior court).

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant's father was of such interest to Ethiopian authorities to persecute claimant; reasons follow.
propositions.quote: The panel is not persuaded that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX's political activities were of such interest to the Ethiopian authorities as to wish to persecute his daughter, the claimant. The panel's reasons follow.

propositions.text: Claimant testified father worked for Ethiopian group and was involved politically; provided documents about his political history and asylum in France.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that XXXXX XXXX XXXXX had worked for the XXXXX XXXXX and was involved in XXXXX XXXXX. She provided a copy of a document 'XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX'10 which lists the XXXX XXXX in Ethiopia in XXXX; XXXXX XXXX XXXXX is listed as XXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (XXX) and 'XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX'. A document provided by the claimant entitled 'Col. Asrat Bogale passed away'11 states that the Colonel left Ethiopia when the Derg military came to power in the 1970s by hijacking an airplane; he was forced to land in Djibouti, jailed for two years and then was given political asylum by the French government. The document also states that he later helped to form the Ethiopian National United Front (ENUF). Other documents provided by the claimant indicate that the Colonel has waged a political campaign from outside Ethiopia for over thirty years.12 Colonel Bogale left Ethiopia in 1977 when the Derg regime was in power; the Derg regime lost power in 1991 when the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) came to power.13 The claimant testified that her father left Ethiopia before she was born. Thus, by 2005, Colonel Bogale had been out of Ethiopia for more than thirty-five years. The EDU party of which Colonel Bogale was a leader in 1995 is one of eighty-six Ethiopian political parties listed in one of the documents referred to above.14 In the article 'Col. Asrat Bogale passed away'15 the ENUF party that the he later helped to form is described as a "clandestine group". The ENUF party is not found in the list of Ethiopian political parties in the 'Annex F: List of registered political parties' in the United Kingdom (UK), 18 January 2008, Home Office XXXX.16 The claimant testified that her father is XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX. She provided a copy of a letter17 from the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The letter is a brief acknowledgement of a letter XXXXX XXXXX wrote to the president of France. There is no persuasive evidence in the letter that XXXXX XXXXX is well known to the president of France or other French authorities.

propositions.text: Panel believes claimant's father is not well known to French authorities and is not a significant political figure.
propositions.quote: The panel believes that the claimant's father, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant carries father's name; panel finds it unreasonable embassy was unaware of relationship when she was recruited.
propositions.quote: The claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX [panel's emphasis], carries her father's name, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX [panel's emphasis]. The claimant testified that she applied for the position with XXXXX through the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX. She testified that she did not know if at that time a thorough check was done on her background. The panel finds it unreasonable that the XXXXXX XXXXXX were not aware of the claimant's relationship with her father when she was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in Paris.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence implies claimant's father was a political exile; independent evidence indicates otherwise.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence provided by the claimant implies that her father was a XXXXXXXXX XXXXX. The independent documentary evidence indicates that

paragraphs.summary: Panel not persuaded claimant's father was politically significant enough to cause persecution; claimant's evidence and documents reviewed; panel finds embassy likely knew relationship (earlier decision-maker and applicant).

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant would face persecution if returned to Ethiopia; evidence reviewed.
propositions.quote: The panel is not persuaded that the claimant was to be returned to Ethiopia to face persecution. The panel has considered the claimant's testimony and the documentary evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant testified she received letter reprimanding her for negligence and letter terminating employment requiring return to Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that she received a letter, dated XXXXX, 2009, from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris reprimanding her for her negligence in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She provided a copy of this document and a translation.26 The claimant testified that she was informed on XXXX, 2009 by letter from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris that her services were no longer required and she was to return to Ethiopia no later than XXXXX, 2009. The claimant provided a copy of this letter and a translation.27

propositions.text: Independent evidence shows embassy staff left posts for refusing to influence diaspora; diplomats recalled and suspended for disloyalty; no evidence of persecution on return.
propositions.quote: The independent documentary evidence does not support the claimant's allegation that she would face persecution in Ethiopia upon return from her XXXXX XXXXX in Paris. The Response to Information Request ETH102458.E 28 focuses specifically on Ethiopians working for the government at embassies outside the country. The Response29 states that staff from various Ethiopian embassies left their posts for refusing to implement plans to influence the Ethiopian diaspora who were in opposition to the Ethiopian government. The Response30 also indicates that Ethiopian diplomats were recalled and suspended for perceived disloyalty to their government. Thus, the panel infers that people in positions such as the claimant's chose to leave the embassies and only diplomats were recalled. There is no indication that any of these people faced persecution upon return to Ethiopia.

propositions.text: No evidence in Response about harsh treatment of embassy staff opposing government; panel expects such evidence if persecution existed.
propositions.quote: The Response31 deals specifically with people working in Ethiopian embassies who returned to Ethiopia because they did not agree with the government. Since there is a plethora of information in other documentary evidence regarding the harsh treatment meted out by the Ethiopian authorities to those who oppose the government32 the panel would expect information in the Response regarding the harsh treatment of people in the Ethiopian embassies who opposed the government if such were the case. There is no such evidence.

propositions.text: Presumption of truthfulness of testimony is rebuttable by failure of documentary evidence to mention expected facts, per Adu.
propositions.quote: The panel is guided by the decision in Adu33 which states that: the 'presumption' that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and , in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimant's testimony about persecution is untrustworthy.
propositions.quote: Thus, the panel concludes that the claimant's testimony in this regard is untrustworthy.

paragraphs.summary: Panel not persuaded claimant would face persecution if returned; documentary evidence reviewed; claimant's testimony found untrustworthy (earlier decision-maker and applicant and prior court).

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant traveled to Canada on holiday and learned of persecution only after arrival; timing suggests otherwise.
propositions.quote: The panel is not persuaded that the claimant travelled to Canada on a holiday and that only after she arrived did she learn that she would be persecuted if she returned to Ethiopia. The timing of events indicates otherwise.

propositions.text: Claimant testified she received letter in Paris requiring return to Ethiopia by a date in 2009.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that, while she was working in Paris, she received a letter informing her that she XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She provided a copy of a letter from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris, dated XXXX, 2009.34 The letter states that her presence at her new workplace in Ethiopia is required no later than XXXX, 2009.

propositions.text: Claimant testified she and family traveled to Canada for holiday, arriving before required return date.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that the reason she and her husband and daughter travelled to Canada was to enjoy a holiday. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2009.35

propositions.text: Claimant testified after arrival she received warning email with attachment from friend of friend in Ethiopian embassy in another city.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that, after she had arrived in Canada, she received a warning e-mail36 with an attachment37 from XXX, a friend of a friend in the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX XXXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges attachment caused her to apply for refugee protection; attachment lacks author, recipient, date, and has no heading or signature.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that it is the information in this attachment that caused her to apply for refugee protection. It is not apparent by whom the attached document38 is written or to whom it is sent; it has no heading, salutation or signature; it has no date.

propositions.text: Panel gives little weight to attachment due to lack of provenance.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the panel gives it little weight.

propositions.text: Panel finds it coincidental claimant had travel visa issued shortly before required return date, traveled to Canada, stayed past return date, then received email prompting refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The panel finds it more than coincidental that the claimant had a travel visa issued XXXXX, 2009, which she used to travel on a holiday to Canada less than a week before she was required to return to Ethiopia for work, remained in Canada after the required return date to Ethiopia, and then received an e-mail from a friend of a friend she happens to know in the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX XXXXX who saw the report [the e-mail attachment]against the claimant which caused the claimant to make a claim for protection on September 1, 2009.

propositions.text: Fortuitous coincidences in applicant's story may justify disbelief, per Federal Court in Ankrah.
propositions.quote: With regard to the coincidences, the panel is guided by the Federal Court decision in Ankrah,39 where J. Noel stated: The applicant's story does otherwise reveal a series of events of chance, and it was open to the tribunal to conclude there from that the Applicant's testimony was too fortuitous in nature to be believed.40

paragraphs.summary: Panel not persuaded claimant traveled to Canada on holiday and learned of persecution only after; attachment lacks provenance; timing is suspicious; Federal Court supports disbelief of fortuitous stories (earlier decision-maker and applicant and prior court).

propositions.text: Claimant's credibility is diminished due to testimony about travel timing and suspicion of opposition.
propositions.quote: The panel finds the claimant's credibility is diminished due to this testimony.

propositions.text: It is not reasonable claimant could travel to Canada less than a week before required return to Ethiopia if suspected of opposing government.
propositions.quote: it is not reasonable that the claimant could travel to Canada less than a week before she was required to return to Ethiopia if, as she alleges, she was suspected of opposing the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant testified she left France for Canada with appropriate travel visa and that opposition knew she would travel.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that she was able to leave France and travel to Canada because she had the appropriate travel visa. When the panel asked the claimant if the XXXXX was aware that she would travel to Canada she testified that it was reasonable that they knew.

propositions.text: Given strict monitoring and scrutiny, it is not reasonable claimant and family were allowed to travel to Canada less than a week before return date.
propositions.quote: Given the strict monitoring of Ethiopian citizens, the treatment in particular of those in opposition to the government,41 that the claimant's activities had come under scrutiny by the XXXXX XXXXX 42 and she was required to return to Ethiopia it is not reasonable that she and her immediately family were allowed to travel to Canada less that a week before she was to asked to return to Ethiopia.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's credibility diminished due to unreasonable travel timing and suspicion of opposition, despite claimant's testimony about visa and awareness.

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant has good grounds to fear persecution upon return to Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: The panel is not persuaded that the claimant has good grounds to fear persecution upon return to Ethiopia.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to obtain evidence from three people who could support her claim and gave unsatisfactory explanations.
propositions.quote: The panel does not find the claimant's explanations satisfactory for not obtaining or attempting to obtain evidence from three people whom allegedly knew something of her claim.

propositions.text: Claimant testified she did not consider or think of asking three people for evidence supporting her claim.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that she had not considered asking her. The claimant was asked why she had not asked her father for evidence. The claimant testified that she didn't think of it.

propositions.text: Rule 744 requires claimant to provide acceptable documents or explain failure to do so.
propositions.quote: Rule 744 of the Refugee Protection Division stipulates that the claimant "must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim." If the claimant does not provide such documents, he/she must be able to explain the reason they were not provided or at least relay what steps were taken to obtain them.

propositions.text: Mohideen Osman decision allows adverse inference from failure to provide corroborating letters without reasonable explanation.
propositions.quote: The panel also refers to the Mohideen Osman decision46 where the Court held that Regarding the failure of the corroborating letters ...where there is no reasonable explanation for material omissions, they can be the basis of an adverse inference and impugn an applicant's credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to provide acceptable documents or reasons for not doing so and is not credible.
propositions.quote: The claimant has failed to provide acceptable documents establishing her claim or acceptable reasons for not doing so. The panel finds the claimant not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant not credible for failing to obtain evidence from three people and not providing acceptable documents or explanations.

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant would face persecution upon return based on family treatment evidence.
propositions.quote: For a further reason, the panel is not persuaded that the claimant was to be returned to Ethiopia to face persecution.

propositions.text: Claimant testified no family members suffered harm by Ethiopian authorities; family received calls and questioning but no ill-treatment.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that none of her family or her husband's family suffered harm at the hands of the Ethiopian authorities. The claimant testified that her family received telephone calls inquiring about her whereabouts and that her mother was questioned at work by the authorities.

propositions.text: Telephone calls and questioning do not rise to level of ill-treatment.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that none of these examples rise to the level of ill-treatment.

propositions.text: Claimant's mother was allowed to travel to France and currently resides there.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that the Ethiopian authorities allowed her mother to travel to France when her father became seriously ill in 2010. She testified that her mother is presently in France.

propositions.text: It is probable claimant's mother was identified as wife of opposition figure and allowed to travel; repressive regime unlikely to allow travel if claimant was wanted.
propositions.quote: The panel believes that it is probable that the claimant's mother was identified as the wife of XXXXX XXXX XXXXX when she was allowed to travel to France. The panel believes that such a repressive regime as that in Ethiopia would not have allowed the claimant's mother to travel outside of the country if the claimant were wanted for serious political opposition activities.

propositions.text: Claimant's credibility is further compromised by these findings.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant's credibility is further compromised.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's family treatment does not indicate persecution and further compromises claimant's credibility.

propositions.text: Panel does not find credible that claimant allowed infant daughter to return to Ethiopia if fearful of authorities.
propositions.quote: The panel does not find it credible that the claimant allowed her infant daughter to return to Ethiopia for six weeks in XXXX 2009 if the claimant was fearful that the Ethiopian authorities believed she opposed them.

propositions.text: Claimant testified officials learned about her father in 2005 and accused her of disobedience and intimidation at work.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that it was late in 2005 that officials learned who her father was and that they accused her of being influenced by his political views. She testified that she had problems with officials who were angry with her and told her she was disobedient because she was unwilling to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She stated that she was intimidated and received verbal abuse each time she went to work at the XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant's husband and daughter returned to Ethiopia in 2009 carrying political literature; claimant minimized this in testimony.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that her husband and daughter returned to Ethiopia in XXXX 2009. She testified that her husband carried her father XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. ... She testified that the authorities had a problem with her, not her child. ... She testified that her husband visited only one store in XXXXX XXXXX that carries lots of opposition media; she explained that her husband brought only one of her father's books thus she didn't think the authorities would put much pressure on her husband.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanations minimizing political literature and safety concerns are not reasonable given knowledge of political situation and government practices.
propositions.quote: The panel does not find the claimant's explanations reasonable. She is well educated. Documentary evidence states that the Ethiopian government uses a widespread system of paid informants to report on the activities of individuals and security forces detain family members of those who oppose the government. According to her PIF narrative and her testimony, she is aware of the political situation in Ethiopia and knowledgeable about her father's experiences with the XXXXX XXXXX.

propositions.text: Panel believes child's safety would be paramount and claimant would not have allowed return if concerned.
propositions.quote: The panel can appreciate that the principal claimant's mother might wish to see her grandchild but the panel believes that the child's safety would be paramount to the claimant. The panel does not believe that the claimant would have allowed her one year old child to return to Ethiopia if she had personal concerns about the XX

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's explanations about allowing infant's return to Ethiopia and political literature are not reasonable and further undermines credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant's behaviour is inconsistent with someone fearful of persecution.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant's behaviour is not that of a person who is fearful of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's behaviour inconsistent with fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Subjective fear is questioned when person voluntarily leaves safe country or fails to seek protection in transit country.
propositions.quote: The question of subjective fear is raised when a person voluntarily leaves a country where he or she could safely live or fails without valid reason to ask for protection in a country through which he or she has travelled.

propositions.text: Presumption that persons fleeing persecution seek protection at first opportunity, usually first country reached.
propositions.quote: There is a presumption that persons fleeing persecution will seek protection at the first opportunity, which would normally be in the first country they reach.

propositions.text: Failure to seek protection in another Convention signatory country is significant for subjective fear assessment.
propositions.quote: Failure to seek the protection of another country which is also a signatory of the Convention may be a significant factor to consider with regard to subjective fear.

propositions.text: Claimant lived in France over four years but did not seek protection there.
propositions.quote: The claimant did not seek protection from the government of France during the more than four years she lived there.

propositions.text: Claimant was interrogated in 2008 after US holiday, suspected of contacting opposition parties.
propositions.quote: the claimant stated that upon her return from a holiday in the United States (US) in 2008 she was interrogated about the purpose of her visit there. She stated that she was suspected of contacting Ethiopian opposition parties in the US.

propositions.text: Claimant argued fear of diplomatic disallowance of claim in France due to employer.
propositions.quote: the claimant testified that, since she worked for the XXXXX XXXXX, she was afraid that a diplomatic approach might be used to disallow the claim.

propositions.text: Claimant provided no persuasive evidence that France would disallow claim diplomatically; father lived safely in France for 30 years.
propositions.quote: The claimant provided no persuasive evidence that this might have been the case. Indeed, her father, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, lived safely in the protection of the French government for over thirty years.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe French government would disallow refugee claim by diplomatic means.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe that the French government would be persuaded to disallow a refugee claim by diplomatic means.

propositions.text: Claimant could have sought protection in France if genuinely feared persecution in Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant could have sought the protection of France if she genuinely feared persecution in Ethiopia.

propositions.text: Safakhoo decision found inconsistency in sojourning in France five years without refugee claim.
propositions.quote: In the decision of Safakhoo the Federal Court found that it was inconsistent with a well-founded fear of persecution that the applicants should sojourn in France for five years without making an application for refugee status.

propositions.text: Mohamed and Omer decision states Convention protects those needing protection, not preference for asylum country.
propositions.quote: In the decision of Hibo Farah Mohamed and Ardo Abdi Omer v. MCI, the Court held: The Geneva Convention exists for persons who require protection and not to assist persons who simply prefer asylum in one country over another.

propositions.text: Assadi decision held failure to immediately seek protection can impugn claimant's credibility.
propositions.quote: Similarly, in the Case of Assadi, Nasser-Eddin v MCI, the Court held: Failure to immediately seek protection can impugn the claimant's credibility, including his or her testimony about events in his country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains legal principles on subjective fear and finds claimant's failure to seek protection in France undermines her fear claim.

propositions.text: Claimant testified suspicion and intimidation by Ethiopian government from 2005 to mid-2009 in France.
propositions.quote: As stated earlier, the claimant testified that she came under the suspicion of the Ethiopian government not long after she arrived in France in 2005 and suffered verbal abuse and intimidation from that time until mid-2009.

propositions.text: Claimant's failure to seek protection in France undermines her subjective fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: The panel determines that the claimant's failure to seek protection in France undermines her subjective fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's failure to seek protection in France undermines her subjective fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Claimant has not established subjective fear of persecution after considering failure to seek protection in France.
propositions.quote: After considering the claimant's failure to seek protection in France, where the claimant had reasonable opportunity to do so, the panel determines that she has not established a subjective fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant has not established subjective fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Panel does not find credible principal claimant's return to Ethiopia with infant and political literature if aware of wife's problems.
propositions.quote: The panel does not find it credible that the principal claimant returned to Ethiopia for six weeks with his infant in XXXX 2009 and with literature of XXXXX XXXXX if he knew that the claimant was fearful that the XXXXX XXXXX believed she opposed them.

propositions.text: Principal claimant testified awareness of wife's problems and carried political literature at mother's insistence, denying political involvement.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant testified that he was aware of his wife's problems with the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris. He testified that he carried the political literature of XXXXX XXXXX because he was asked to. He further explained that he was not involved in any political activities;

propositions.text: Panel finds principal claimant's explanations unreasonable given knowledge of government informants and wife's problems.
propositions.quote: The panel does not find the principal claimant's explanations reasonable. He is well educated with seventeen years of formal education. Documentary evidence states that the Ethiopian government uses a widespread system of paid informants to report on the activities of individuals and security forces detain family members of those who oppose the government.

propositions.text: Panel believes principal claimant would prioritize child's safety and not carry opposition literature if aware of problems.
propositions.quote: The panel can appreciate that the principal claimant's mother might wish to see her grandchild but the panel believes that the child's safety would be vital to the principal claimant. The panel does not believe that the principal claimant would have carried literature opposing the Ethiopian authorities and taken his one year old child to Ethiopia if he was aware of the principal claimant's problems with XXXXX XXXXX.

propositions.text: Principal claimant's behaviour inconsistent with genuine fear of persecution; testimony untrustworthy.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant's behaviour is not consistent with that of someone genuinely fearing removal to a place of persecution. The panel finds the principal claimant's testimony in this regard untrustworthy.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds principal claimant's explanations unreasonable and behaviour inconsistent with genuine fear, rendering testimony untrustworthy.

propositions.text: Claimant is not credible and has not met burden to establish serious possibility of persecution for Convention ground.
propositions.quote: After considering all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is not credible and has, therefore, not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted for a Convention ground.

propositions.text: Cumulative credibility concerns on central issues negate claim despite no single concern being sufficient alone.
propositions.quote: The panel is aware that none of the credibility concerns raised here may be sufficient, each on its own, to negate this claim. However, given that these concerns touch upon such important, central issues in the claim, the cumulative effect is that the panel does not have sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that the claimant is a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is not credible and fails to establish serious possibility of persecution due to cumulative concerns.

propositions.text: Claimant provided no persuasive evidence of risk of torture under Convention Against Torture.
propositions.quote: The claimant advanced no persuasive evidence to suggest she would face any danger, that is, more likely than not, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant provided no persuasive evidence of risk of torture under the Convention Against Torture.

propositions.text: Claimant lacks subjective fear and is not at risk of cruel or unusual treatment if returned to Ethiopia.
propositions.quote: Given the findings above, that the claimant is not a credible witness and lacks subjective fear, the panel finds that she is not a person who faces a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she were to return to Ethiopia.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant lacks subjective fear and is not at risk of cruel or unusual treatment if returned to Ethiopia.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the claimant is not a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is not a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Claimant and dependents are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The principal claimant and the minor claimant depend upon the claim of XXXXX XXXX XXXXX. Therefore, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXX are also not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant and dependents are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA.
